title: Two messages, same job
text:
Two messages. Same job.

A: "I'm very passionate about this opportunity and believe I'd be a great fit."

B: "Your posting says onboarding has to get faster before the Q1 launch. At my last company I cut ours from 3 weeks to 9 days. Worth 15 minutes next week?"

A is about you. B is about them.

Hiring managers can tell which is which before they finish the first line.

Before you hit send, ask one question: could I paste this into another company's inbox without changing a word? If yes, rewrite it.

title: Which person to email first
text:
They're right about the email.

There's a post going around on how to get job offers. Its advice: stop relying on applications, catch hiring posts while they're fresh, and email the person who posted the job. Keep it plain, because "short, direct, slightly messy emails stand out."

I agree. But it leaves out the hard part: which person to write to, and what to say.

Every job has four people who decide whether you get it. Each one needs a different note.

The hiring manager feels the empty seat. Name one problem their team has (the posting usually tells you), add one line of proof you can help, and ask one easy question.

Their boss approved the role. Say why their team's goal is the one you want to work on, and keep it shorter.

Someone on the team knows what the job really needs. Ask one real question about the work. Not for a referral, not yet.

The recruiter runs the process. Say you applied and why: the role, one line on fit, and when you're free to talk.

Four people, four short notes, each in your own words.

That's the method I used to land jobs at ClickUp, Deel and Google, and it's what we built Day60 to run: it finds the four people for one job and drafts a first note to each. You rewrite it until it sounds like you, then you send it.

Being good at the work still matters most. This just gets the right people to see it.

title: Write the next step first
text:
Write the next step before you hang up.

A lot of first calls end with "let's stay in touch" or "I'll send something over." Two weeks later, nobody remembers what was agreed.

Before the call ends:

1. Say the next step out loud: what happens, who does it, by when.
2. Put a time on both calendars while you're still on the line.
3. Send a three-line recap within the hour: what you heard, what you agreed, the date.

A call without a next step isn't pipeline yet. It's a conversation.

What's the last thing you say before you hang up?

1. Could it only go to this team?

title: The ATS probably didn't reject you
text:
The ATS probably didn't reject you.

The story goes like this: a robot read your resume, frowned at the font, and tossed it before any human saw it.

Most applicant tracking systems don't work that way. They store and organize applications, and recruiters search them by keyword when they're ready to look.

What can screen you out early is the form itself: knockout questions about work authorization, location or years of experience. That's the form, not your layout.

"ATS-friendly" and "beat the ATS" are mostly sales language. What helps is simpler: use the posting's own words where they're true for you, and make sure a person knows you applied.

So if no one has replied, the likely reason isn't a robot. No person has looked yet.

That part you can change. Find the hiring manager and send three lines: one problem their team has, one line of proof, one easy question. I built Day60 to find the 4 people closest to the hire, so that note has somewhere to go.

title: Nobody calls a company
text:
In sales development, nobody calls a company.

You call a person. A company can't say yes. A person can.

I founded ClickUp's sales development team, and that's still the idea I'd keep if I could keep only one.

Job seekers get taught the opposite. Apply to the company. Wait for the company. Hope the company writes back.

So before your next application, answer two questions:
1. Who would I report to?
2. What problem is that person trying to solve right now?

If you can't answer the second one yet, that's your homework before you write a word.

It's the idea I built Day60 around.

title: Five stages of waiting
text:
The five stages of waiting for a reply:

1. Refresh.
2. Refresh again, just in case.
3. Draft a follow-up. Delete it. Too soon.
4. Wonder if the email ever arrived.
5. Refresh.

Anyone who has worked in sales has lived all five.

What fixes it isn't patience. It's a plan you set before you hit send: on day 2, a short note with something new. On day 7, a kind last word. Then stop.

Three touches is persistence. Ten is spam. And when you know when the next one is due, you can stop refreshing.
